note: Everything the Orange Pi Zero 3 (4x A53 @ 1.5 GHz, 1.5 GB) is allowed to run, and what each thing may cost. CLAUDE.md rule 20: the board carries only what is real-time critical or must survive a WiFi loss or is wired to its own pins; everything that consumes the camera lives on the laptop. Nothing is added to the board without an entry here with a measured budget (pepin.census reads this file; ros/board.sh census compares it against a live ps). Budgets are today's measurement +50 % unless the entry's note says the number is a guess. The measurement is ps's %CPU, which is the process's average over its whole life, not an instant sample: read a census taken in the first minute after a start as start-up cost, not as the running cost (the census prints the age of the youngest process for that reason). Percentages are of ONE core: 400 % is the whole board. Census of 2026-09-14 12:40 EDT, stack up 2 min 22 s, nav:=true imu:=true tof:=true neck:=true side:=all, load 7.3. Since 2026-10-01 the board is a sensor box: Nav2, the goal server and the drive recorders run on the laptop.

ignore.why: kernel threads (kworker, SPRDWL/sdiohal for the WiFi-over-SDIO, ksoftirqd): no RSS, not started by us, not ours to budget. They do cost real CPU — the WiFi threads alone run 5-8 % — which is why the manifest promises well under 400 %.
the ssh session the census itself arrives on
the census's own ps and the shell around it (they read 300-400 % because they lived for a fraction of a second)
the ros2 CLI's discovery daemon, spawned by our own probes (ros/tools/topic_rate.py, flags.sh); idle between calls

processes.name: lidar_container
processes.role: The lidar in a process of its own at high priority, respawned 2 s after it dies: the LD19 driver, the hull filter that makes /scan, its static mount and the lifecycle manager that activates the driver. A lidar that dies must not take the base with it (2026-09-24).

components.name: scan_filter
components.role: cuts the cart's own hull out of the scan and republishes /scan

processes.note: Measured 12-13 % / 62-75 MB on 2026-09-24 (the respawn tests of that night included); split from sensors_container (21 % / 60 MB for everything). Each process carries its own zenoh session (~40 MB).

processes.name: base_container
processes.role: The base in a process of its own at high priority, respawned 2 s after it dies: the wheel bridge (cmd_vel in, odom and the IMU's yaw rate out, the gyro's zero re-measured at rest, a zero-velocity update for the EKF while the cart is certainly still, the neck's encoders as /neck/state and base_link -> camera_link).

components.name: base_bridge
components.role: wheel speeds and odometry over TCP 3336, /cmd_vel in, /odom out, the MPU6050's yaw rate as imu/data_raw whose zero is re-measured from the rest the wheels witness, and /zupt (the EKF's odom2, a zero twist at 10 Hz) while that rest, no fresh cmd_vel and a quiet gyro agree; the neck's ticks riding every state line as /neck/state and base_link -> camera_link at that line's stamp, 50 Hz (ros/pepin_base_cpp, neck.hpp)

processes.note: Measured 5-6 % / 43-54 MB on 2026-09-24, 5.4 % on 2026-10-01 (state lines at 16.7 Hz, gyro at 50); split from sensors_container. Each process carries its own zenoh session (~40 MB). With 50 state lines and 100 gyro reads a second, AN ESTIMATE until a census: ~11 % (the lines +0.76 % of a laptop core in a replica, x4.4; the gyro loop doubled). Since 2026-10-02 it also publishes the neck (a JointState and a transform per state line, 50 Hz), which retired pepin_bringup.neck_state (measured 10 % / 66 MB in a process of its own): AN ESTIMATE until a census, +2-3 % here, about the cost of the /odom it publishes beside them; the budget stays.

processes.name: bag_record
processes.role: rosbag2 writing MCAP: the board's own always-on recording of its raw sensors under /maps/board_rec when PEPIN_BOARD_BAG=true (pepin.board_bag, started and capped by the board_bag entry), or a recorded drive's bag in /maps/rec (ros/teleop.sh NAME). Generic subscriptions: messages are copied as serialised bytes and nothing on this board deserialises a scan.
processes.owner: pepin.board_bag (pepin-ros.service -> robot.launch.py board_bag:=true, nice 10); ros/teleop.sh NAME (docker exec in pepin-ros)
processes.note: The board recording (board_bag), AN ESTIMATE until a census with it on: 5.1-6.4 % of a laptop core and 70 MB in a network-isolated replica (drive 0576 replayed, the wheels at 50 Hz, the gyro at 100, ~300 messages and 0.14 MB/s), x4.4 the EKF's board/laptop ratio: ~25 %. Per message, not per byte: MCAP's fastwrite preset changed nothing, 50 messages a second fewer (/odometry/filtered, dropped) took 15 %. A teleop drive's bag was never measured.

processes.name: board_bag
processes.role: The supervisor of the board's raw-sensor recording: keeps one `ros2 bag record` running (minute MCAP files under /maps/board_rec) and deletes the oldest minutes past 20 GB or when the card has under 10 GB free; a card still under the floor stops the recorder.
processes.owner: pepin-ros.service -> robot.launch.py (board_bag:=true, ros/feature.sh board_bag on), nice 10, respawned
processes.note: Measured 0.02 % of a laptop core / 15 MB in a network-isolated container: a stdlib Python loop that lists a directory every 30 s.

processes.name: tof_bridge
processes.role: Publishes the three VL53L1X ranges from the ToF server as ROS Range messages for the costmaps' contact layer.
processes.note: Measured 13 % / 68 MB. An rclpy process costs ~65 MB before it does anything. The tf_gate of 2026-09-21 put an rclpy TF listener in here and took it to 20-37 % of a core; it came out on 2026-09-22 (the whiskers reach Nav2 as scan fans instead), so the next census should read 13 % again.

processes.name: laser_odometry
processes.role: Laser odometry: matches each LD19 scan against the one before it (rf2o, scan to scan, no map) and publishes /odom_laser, which the EKF fuses as a twist (odom3). The one odometry input a wheel spinning on carpet cannot fool.
processes.note: TO MEASURE: every number here is an estimate and the first census after this feature lands replaces it. Where it comes from: RF2O's paper reports 0.9 ms per scan on one desktop core at 1080 beams; ours are 455, and an A53 at 1.5 GHz with no tuned SIMD is taken at 10x a desktop core, so 4-8 ms of the 100 ms between scans -> 4-8 %, +50 % -> 12, rounded to 20 because nothing is measured. The memory is a C++ ROS node's measured 28 MB (ekf_node) plus the ~40 MB of zenoh session every process on this board carries, and the same headroom. If the census says OVER, the honest lever is the node's freq, not this number.

processes.name: ekf_node
processes.role: Fuses the wheels and the gyro in the plane and owns odom -> base_link (the wheels over-report rotation on carpet, the gyro does not).
processes.note: Measured 9 % / 28 MB; 12 % on 2026-10-01 at 20 Hz with the wheels at 16.7 Hz and the gyro at 50 (sensors-only board, ps over 38 min). 50 Hz with the wheels at 50 and the gyro at 100 is AN ESTIMATE until a census measures it: 1.9x in a network-isolated replica of its inputs (2.78 -> 5.28 % of a laptop core; 1.34x for the 50 Hz filter and wheels alone, 2.9x with a 200 Hz gyro), so ~23 %.

processes.name: ros2_launch
processes.role: The launch process itself: it started every ROS node above and respawns the ones that may come back alone.
processes.note: Measured 7 % / 70 MB on 2026-09-14, when it also started Nav2. One launch process for every node, on purpose: two cost ~110 MB of Python each.

processes.name: zenoh_router
processes.role: The board's half of the rmw_zenoh transport: the one process that carries this board's graph to the laptop's router. Board-internal traffic does NOT pass through it — every node here is a zenoh peer of every other over the host loopback (measured 0.0 % router CPU for a 10 Hz x 100 kB board-internal flow, against 1.4 % with the same two nodes as clients).
processes.note: Measured 12 % on 2026-10-01 (sensors-only board, ps over 38 min). The 50 Hz wheels, the 50 Hz filter and the 100 Hz gyro add ~7 % more to what it forwards to the laptop, AN ESTIMATE until a census: 1.7 -> 3.4 % of a laptop core in a replica (a board router forwarding /odom, /imu/data_raw, /tf and /odometry/filtered to a laptop router and its client), x4.4.

processes.name: chronyd
processes.role: The board's clock (board/chrony.sh, installed with `ros/time.sh install`): follows the laptop's time server — the Docker VM's clock, which every laptop ROS node stamps with — and keeps the internet pool as its fallback and its vote. Replaces systemd-timesyncd; `ros/time.sh uninstall` puts that back.
processes.note: A GUESS until the first census after the install: one small C daemon, one 48-byte UDP exchange with the laptop every 4-16 s and with each pool server every 1-17 min. `sometimes` because it exists only after `ros/time.sh install` (the board runs systemd-timesyncd until then, below the unlisted threshold). It stays on the board because the board's own clock must keep going when the WiFi and the laptop are gone: it free-runs on the frequency it learned.

processes.name: base_server
processes.role: The wheels next to the UART: speed commands, odometry ticks and the deadman, on TCP 3336. The last thing between a runaway and a stopped cart.
processes.note: Measured 10 % / 18 MB; 8.5 % on 2026-10-01 at 16.7 state lines a second. 50 a second (every tick) adds an estimated 2-3 %: +0.56 % of a laptop core for the lines and two readers over a fake bus (scratch bench, x4.4 the EKF's board/laptop ratio). Since 2026-10-02 the neck rides the tick: two more ids in the one encoder read (+0.18 ms of wire), at most one unacknowledged neck write a tick, two ints in the state line; the neck node's 2-20 Hz `neck` polls are gone. Outside Docker on purpose: it must survive a container restart.

processes.name: tof_server
processes.role: Streams the three VL53L1X ranges over TCP 3335 from the I2C bus.
processes.owner: pepin-tof.service (/opt/pepin, systemd; tof-init.service re-addresses the sensors first)
processes.note: Measured 9 % / 15 MB.

processes.name: audio_server
processes.role: The XVF3800 array's processed voice out and the speaker's playback in, over TCP 3338.
processes.note: Measured 1.6 % / 20 MB idle and 2.0 % / 20 MB with a client listening (2026-10-02).

processes.name: head_server
processes.role: Owns the head ESP32's serial port (/dev/pepin-head, CH340 at 921600 baud) on TCP 3340: the mouth's expressions, speech levels and info screens down; the head IMU's samples up, mapped onto the board's clock and streamed to the base bridge; the brain lease.
processes.note: TO MEASURE on the board: an ESTIMATE until the head is plugged in. Bench on the Mac (2026-10-03, the real server against a byte-accurate virtual ESP32 on a pty, one subscriber, 10 s each): at the default 200 Hz in 20 ms frames (50 frames/s) the loop thread takes 0.65 % of an M5 core (port reads 0.20 %, frames 0.31 %, commands 0.08 %, ticks 0.06 %; 10 ms read timeout); at 1 kHz in 5-sample frames (200 frames/s, before the 20 ms frames) 1.84 %; RSS 28 MB. At the x4.4 laptop-to-board ratio base_server's note uses, 200 Hz is ~3 %, at x10 ~7 %: 8 % is the budget. Levers if the census says OVER: a longer read timeout, or longer frames in imu.cpp (batch_n). Outside Docker on purpose, like base_server: the face and the IMU must survive a container restart, and the face falls asleep on WiFi loss by the lease rather than by dying.

processes.name: ser2net
processes.role: The servo bus and the lidar as TCP ports (3333/3334) so the laptop's tools can reach them without a serial cable.
processes.note: Measured 4 % / 3 MB.

processes.name: ustreamer
processes.role: The overview camera as MJPEG on http 8080: the one camera consumer that stays on the board, because it only copies frames out of the USB stack and never decodes them.
processes.owner: pepin-camera.service (on the board only; the unit is not yet in board/)
processes.note: Measured 2 % / 13 MB at 1280x720, 15 fps, --drop-same-frames 30. The image is passed through, not encoded; anything that LOOKS at these frames (depth, scans, matching) belongs on the laptop — rule 20.

processes.name: docker
processes.role: The container runtime and one supervisor per container: what keeps pepin-ros and the router alive across a crash.
processes.note: Measured ~1 % total and ~150 MB across dockerd, containerd, two shims and the pepin-ros `docker run`. Memory, not CPU, is what it costs us.

processes.name: journald
processes.role: The host's journal: every unit's output and the kernel's messages, written to the SD card (the board's services log through it; the containers' own logs stay in docker's files).
processes.note: Measured 1.4-2 % / 9 MB on 2026-09-24, over the 1 % an unlisted process may cost, so every census that night was red on it; listed so that a journal that starts to churn shows as OVER instead of as noise.

processes.name: reap_ros2_cli
processes.role: Every minute, kills ros2 CLI tools older than 90 s left inside the container — a dozen leftovers took the board to load 12 on 2026-09-13.
processes.note: A guess: the oneshot lives under a second and a census almost never catches it. Its point is that it is cheap and that a census that DOES catch it should not go red.

processes.name: session_logger
processes.role: The recorded teleop run's recorder, started by ros/teleop.sh NAME: scans, odometry, pose and commands into one jsonl for the post-drive plots.
processes.owner: started inside the pepin-ros container by ros/teleop.sh NAME (ros/tools/session_logger.py)
processes.note: A guess: it has never been measured on its own, and it only runs during a drive, which is when the board is busiest. Measure it on the next recorded drive and replace this number.

processes.name: foxglove_bridge
processes.role: The Foxglove websocket. Being removed: the laptop reads the board through the zenoh routers, and a second serialiser of every topic is a luxury on four A53 cores.
processes.owner: none: robot.launch.py composes no Foxglove bridge since 2026-10-02 (it sat behind foxglove:=true, off since 2026-09-14)
processes.note: Not expected on the board: the laptop runs one Foxglove bridge and it sees the board through the zenoh routers. If a process with this name appears, someone started one by hand.
